title: Deliberate Practice for Ten Thousand Hours Makes a Genius
author: Tongren Yuye
excerpt: (Original title: How to Practice for Ten Thousand Hours)

inline.s: (Original title: How to Practice for Ten Thousand Hours)

With the popularity of the bestselling book Outliers, the slogan “ten thousand hours of deliberate practice makes a genius” is now known to everyone. Perhaps many still believe that those once-in-a-generation geniuses must possess some innate mysterious ability, but scientists, through extensive investigation, have reached a consensus:
all top performers are made through practice
. What is more, with scientific progress in recent years, people may for the first time possess
a unified theory of how geniuses are made

[Ten thousand hours of deliberate practice makes a genius] In his book Outliers, the writer Gladwell points out: “The reason the geniuses in people's eyes are so extraordinary is not that they are gifted beyond ordinary people, but that they have made sustained, unremitting effort. Ten thousand hours of tempering is the necessary condition for anyone to go from ordinary to extraordinary.” He calls this the “ten-thousand-hour rule.” [Ten thousand hours] In a year of 365 days, practicing deliberately three hours a day takes about ten years (9.1 years to be precise); practicing deliberately six hours a day takes about five years (4.6 years to be precise).

The good news is that, apart from certain sports that have special requirements for innate height and build, mysterious inborn talent does not exist — that is to say, everyone can potentially become a top performer. More than twenty years ago, the University of Chicago education scholar Benjamin Bloom closely studied 120 elite figures across fields from music to mathematics and found that there was nothing special about them in early childhood. Later research further showed that in many fields even IQ has nothing to do with whether a person can reach expert level.
A Hungarian psychologist long ago believed that with the right method, any person could be trained into a top performer in any field.

To prove this, he chose a pursuit traditionally unsuited to women — chess. In the end, he and his wife trained all three of their daughters into world-class chess masters: the famous Polgár sisters. This experiment even shows that you can be trained into a master of a field even if you do not love it, for one of the three sisters did not particularly like chess.

The bad news is that becoming a master requires long practice. Practicing three hours a day, completing ten thousand hours takes ten years, and this is only the minimum requirement for reaching world-class level.
Statistics show that for musicians, the training time required for world-class level is fifteen to twenty-five years. But the most crucial thing is not the time spent practicing,
but the method of practice

How is a genius made? Traditional Chinese thinking tends to emphasize a single word, “bitterness”: practice in the coldest days of winter and the hottest days of summer, even tying one's hair to a beam or pricking one's thigh with an awl. As modern life has grown more comfortable, people have begun to emphasize a word, “love,” saying that interest is the best teacher and stressing learning through joy; the parents of the “Harvard girls” have written books one after another describing how their children
played their way into elite schools

Many inspirational stories and popular success books love above all to emphasize “sudden enlightenment,” holding that a person fails only because he has not figured things out, because he has not recognized his true self! It is as if, once a person has an epiphany about his true self, he will very simply become a genius in the field that is truly his own. A salesman may think his true self is actually a novelist, a doctor may think his true self is actually a painter — the only problem being that they have never written a novel or painted a picture — yet they think they are only one step away from “their true self,” and that once they try they will burst forth as geniuses.
All these personal experiences and inspirational stories about the science of success
are unscientific
. Suppose a successful person has done a hundred things — entering speech contests, dressing with individuality, listening to English songs, liking green best, and so on —
he will very complacently write all hundred of them into his autobiography
, and perhaps add the influence of a girlfriend. Yet among them, what truly played a decisive role may be
only four things
, and the problem is that neither he nor his readers know which four.

[Only four things] These four things are the four requirements of deliberate practice spoken of below: 1. practice only in the “learning zone”; 2. massive repetition; 3. continuously obtain effective feedback; 4. intense mental concentration.
Scientists do not believe inspirational stories; they believe only in investigation and research.

Over the past twenty or thirty years, psychologists have systematically studied the training methods of everyone from novices and ordinary experts to world-class masters in all trades and professions — athletes, musicians, chess players, doctors, mathematicians, people with extraordinary memories, and so on — trying to discover the common elements. Their research even went so far as to precisely record every little thing all the students at a music conservatory did each day, how much time they spent on each thing, and their parents and family circumstances, in order to compare what exactly makes those musical geniuses stand out.
By now this work has matured. In 2006, a book of over nine hundred pages, The Cambridge Handbook of Expertise and Expert Performance, was published. It is
“how geniuses are made”
research — a landmark scholarly work, and it directly led to the appearance of a series of later bestsellers, including Gladwell's
Outliers

, Geoff Colvin's Talent is Overrated, and Daniel Coyle's The Talent Code, among others. Scientists have not only proved that top performers are made through practice, but, by examining the common elements of the best training methods in every field, have summed up a unified method of practice — the so-called
“deliberate practice”

Over the years, training methods have continually advanced. Take composition, for example. Suppose a level that an ordinary student reaches in six years with ordinary methods, another student reaches in three years with new methods; then we can say the “
effectiveness index

” of the new method is 200%. Statistics show that Mozart's training at the time had an effectiveness index of 130%. The geniuses of the twentieth century may be less famous than Mozart, but their training levels could all reach 300% to 500%! The seventeenth-century philosopher Bacon once held that no one could master mathematics in fewer than thirty years, yet today's students have learned far more mathematics by their teens —
teaching methods have advanced!
In fact, we do better in every field today than in the past: world records in sport are continually broken, and artists' skills are beyond anything the past could have imagined.
Another manifestation of the importance of training methods is the
clustering

of “geniuses”: for example, there was a time when Russia dominated women's tennis and Korea women's field hockey, not to mention China's absolute dominance in table tennis. Going further, even if your country is not traditionally good at a sport,
as long as one coach gropes his way to and masters scientific training methods, he can bring forth a generation of peerless champions

, such as China's figure-skating coach Yao Bin. People often lament that China, with its billion-plus people, cannot find eleven football geniuses — if genius were inborn, then a billion-plus people would surely be enough to produce many geniuses,
but genius is made through practice
, and China lacks
an effective environment for practice
; no matter how large the population, it cannot compare with a small European country.
The first to propose the concept of “deliberate practice” was K. Anders Ericsson, a psychologist at the University of Florida. The core hypothesis of this method of practice is that

expert-level ability is built up gradually through practice, and that the key to effective progress lies in finding a series of small tasks for the trainee to complete in order. These small tasks must be ones the trainee happens not to be able to do, yet is just able to learn and master.
Completing this kind of practice requires intense mental concentration, which is entirely different from those routine or entertainment-flavored exercises. The theory of “
deliberate practice
” is now widely accepted, and we can sum up its characteristics.

Scientists who studied the training of figure skaters found that in the same amount of practice time, ordinary athletes prefer to practice moves they have long since mastered, while top athletes practice more of the various high-difficulty jumps. Ordinary amateurs play golf purely to enjoy the process, while professional players concentrate on practicing difficult shots from all kinds of extremely uncomfortable positions. Real practice is not for completing a training quota, nor for enjoying the process;
the essence of practice is to keep doing what one is not yet good at

Psychologists divide a person's knowledge and skills into three adjacent concentric rings: the innermost ring is the “comfort zone,” the skills we have already mastered; the outermost ring is the “panic zone,” the skills we cannot yet learn; the ring between the two is the “learning zone.”
Only by practicing in the learning zone can a person make progress.
Effective practice tasks
must be carried out precisely
within the trainee's “learning zone,”
with a high degree of specificity
. In many cases this requires a good teacher or coach, who, from the standpoint of an observer, is better able to
spot where we most need improvement

. (Editor's note: Whenever the learning zone becomes the comfort zone, one must immediately move into a new learning zone — that is, the former panic zone — and a panic zone of still greater difficulty correspondingly appears. In this way one advances ring by ring, climbing the peak step by step. Never sink into stagnation on the path; this is what is meant by “knowing the turning points.”)

Practicing only in the learning zone is a very demanding requirement. An ordinary school classroom often has dozens of people learning knowledge at the same pace, and such learning has no specificity. The same content is, for some students, a comfort zone that needs no further practice, while for others it is a panic zone. Scientific teaching must teach according to aptitude, in small classes, or even one-on-one. The training of a true master is, rather than a teacher teaching students,
better described as a master taking on an apprentice

Once one has learned something, one should not keep spending time on it, but should immediately move to the next level of difficulty. Training this way over the long term is bound to yield twice the result for half the effort.
A 2004 study showed that university students' grades had no direct relationship to the total time they invested in study —
the key is the method of study!
The secret of going from not knowing to knowing is repetition

. In California there is a “Shyness Clinic” that specifically helps people who, say, dare not speak to the opposite sex to overcome their shyness. The psychologists at this clinic do not believe in suggestion therapy or childhood memories and the like;
they believe in practice
. They hold that what makes a person shy is not the thing itself,
but our view of the thing
. How does one treat the fear of women?
The method is to design conversation-training situations of various degrees of difficulty

. At first there is group conversation and role-play in a room. Then one goes straight out to the street to strike up a conversation with a beautiful stranger and ask for a date. The highest difficulty is deliberately doing something embarrassing in public, such as dropping a watermelon on the floor of a supermarket and breaking it.
This method of repeating uncommon, high-difficulty events is precisely the essence of the MBA curriculum

. In a business school, a student may face twenty real business cases each week: the students first study how to make the decision themselves, propose solutions, and finally the teacher gives the actual outcome and comments. The best way to learn business decision-making is not to watch one's boss make two decisions a month, but to make twenty simulated decisions a week oneself. The
simulated battles
of military academies, pilots simulating all kinds of rare in-flight emergencies on computers, and even Churchill practicing speeches in front of a mirror — all are repetition training.
In sports and music training, more emphasis is placed on
“blocked” practice
. First you run through the whole movement or the whole piece once, to see how the expert does it.
Then you break it into many small blocks and learn and master them one by one.
In this kind of training one must be slow; only by slowing down can one perceive
the internal structure of the skill and notice one's own mistakes

. At one of America's best violin schools, students are even forbidden to play a piece straight through, on the rule that if others can tell what piece you are playing, it means you have not practiced correctly. Professional sports training is often
aimed at technique, not at the match itself
. A high-level American football player spends only 1% of his time in intra-team matches;
all the rest is various related basic training

Conversely, without such advance repetition training, a person often does not know what to do when faced with an uncommon event. Statistics show that doctors who have worked for years diagnose rare diseases by reading X-rays at a level inferior to that of newly graduated medical students — because they rarely encounter such cases, and what they learned in medical school has long been forgotten. The best approach is actually to
regularly
have doctors train intensively on old X-rays from the past, rather than hoping to come across them in their work.

What is the greatest use of a teacher or coach? Perhaps for most people, the greatest effect of a primary-school teacher is to have sparked their interest in learning and taught them something, having once “propagated the doctrine, imparted knowledge, and resolved doubts.”
But true masters all have a strong capacity for self-study
, and for them
the most important role of a teacher and coach is to provide immediate feedback
Whether a movement is done well or badly, it is best to have a coach
point it out at any moment; the practitioner must be able to know the result of his practice at any moment
Practice whose results cannot be seen is the same as no practice
: if one merely goes through the motions, one will not only fail to improve, but will cease to care about good and bad. To some extent, deliberate practice is
practice centered on error
The practitioner must build up an extreme sensitivity to error; once he finds he has erred, he will feel very uncomfortable, and he keeps practicing until he corrects it.

From the standpoint of training, what is a truly good coach like? John Wooden is the most legendary college basketball coach in America, having led the UCLA team to ten NCAA championships in twelve years. To learn Wooden's coaching secrets, two psychologists once observed his training sessions throughout, even recording every instruction he gave his players. The statistics showed that of the 2,326 instructions recorded, 6.9% were praise and 6.6% expressions of dissatisfaction,
while 75% were pure information — what movement to make and how to make it
. His most common method was a three-part demonstration: demonstrate the correct movement once, perform the wrong movement once, then demonstrate the correct movement once more.
Contrary to what outsiders imagine, the best coaches never deliver passionate speeches, and do not even lecture, never speaking for more than twenty seconds. They give their students only
very specific, immediate feedback
All training is planned in advance in the most minute detail
, even down to teaching athletes how to tie their shoelaces.
They seem to have an uncanny ability to know what their students are thinking, and can point out what a student most needs technically even at the first meeting.
They teach absolutely according to each student's aptitude,
providing an unending stream of highly targeted, specific guidance
The highest state of obtaining feedback is
being one's own coach
When a master works, he observes himself from the standpoint of a bystander, has very specific small goals each day, is extremely sensitive to his own errors, and continually seeks improvement.
Deliberate practice has no concept of “learning through joy.” A famous violinist once said that if you are practicing your fingers, you can practice all day;
but if you are practicing your brain, two hours a day is already doing well

. A master's practice lasts at most 1 to 1.5 hours at a time, and at most 4 to 5 hours a day. No one can endure more. Ordinary female fans may think stars like Beckham are adorable; what they may not know is that very few players can complete Beckham's
training intensity
, because it is simply too grueling.

Scientists once studied a music conservatory. They divided all its violin students into three groups: good (future music teachers), better, and best (future performers). The students in the three groups were alike in many respects — for example, they all began practicing around age eight, and even the total weekly time of music-related activities (lessons, study, practice) was the same, fifty-one hours.
The researchers found that all the students understood one principle: what truly determines your level is not the group music class, but practice alone:
⊙ The students in the two best groups averaged 24 hours of solo practice a week, while the third group had only 9 hours.
⊙ They all regarded solo practice as the most difficult and least enjoyable activity.

⊙ The students in the two best groups did their solo practice in the later part of the morning and the early part of the afternoon, when they were still alert; while the third group practiced in the later part of the afternoon, when they were already drowsy.
⊙ The two best groups not only practiced more, but also slept more. They also napped more.

Then what factor distinguished the first two groups? It was the students' total historical practice time. By age eighteen, the students in the best group had practiced an average of 7,410 hours in all, the second group 5,301 hours, and the third group 3,420 hours. The people in the second group now work as hard as the best group, but it is already too late. From this one can see that to become a world-class master one must begin training early — this is why genius musicians all start practicing from a very young age.

Modern neuroscience and cognitive science hold that there is almost no skill that a person is born knowing. Even simple actions like recognizing simple objects and grasping things are the results of an infant's postnatal learning. When a person is born, he cannot possibly foresee what skills he will need in the future; genes cannot program all skills in advance by heredity, for that would waste too much of the brain's storage space. The best approach is not to preset any skill, but to provide only an ability to learn various skills — this is the ingenuity of the human brain. What genes do is preset some basic responses and sensations to stimuli — for example, seeing something delicious makes us hungry. These basic responses need to mobilize few nerves. But for higher-level skills, such as playing music, which require the coordination of many nerves, one must rely on postnatal learning.

Any skill of a person is a combination of electrical pulse signals transmitted by a series of nerve fibers in the brain. Dissection shows that people with different skills have very different neural structures in their brains — for example, the region for recognizing direction is particularly developed in the brain of a taxi driver.
In other words, unlike a computer, a person's mastery of a skill is realized at the hardware level of the brain

And a school of scientists has recently held that myelin is the key to skill training. Its function is to wrap these nerve fibers the way rubber wraps electrical wires, making the signal stronger, faster, and more accurate by preventing the leakage of electrical impulses. Whatever we practice, we are practicing the myelin in our brains, as if a jumble of wires were being arranged into a cable. It was not until 2000, when new technology allowed scientists to observe myelin directly inside living brains, that its role was discovered, and not until 2006 that it was first explained in an academic journal. Scientists hold that myelin is the expressway of the brain's nerves, raising the speed of signal transmission, and that it can reduce delay time thirtyfold — a total speedup of three thousand times — and can even control the speed, slowing it down at will.
The human brain contains a great deal of “free” myelin, which observes the firing and combination of signals in the brain's nerve fibers; the more a nerve fiber is used,
the more this myelin goes over and wraps that section of the circuit, making signal transmission in the circuit faster and forming an expressway
This is why practice is so important
The myelin theory can explain many things

. For example, why do children often make mistakes? Their nervous systems are all there, and they know right from wrong; they just need time to build up the myelin expressway network. Why is a habit, once formed, hard to change? Because a so-called “habit” is in fact “grown” into the brain in the form of a combination of nerve-fiber cables; once myelin has wrapped the nerves, it does not automatically unwrap —
the only way to change a habit is to form a new habit

. Why do young people learn fast? Because although myelin grows throughout a person's life, it grows fastest in the young. The most radical theory holds that the most notable difference between humans and monkeys lies not in the number of brain neurons, but in the fact that humans have 20% more myelin than monkeys! Dissection shows that the number of neurons in Einstein's brain was average, but he had more cells capable of producing myelin.

blocks.text: 3. Who Is Willing to Practice Deliberately for Ten Thousand Hours?

inline.s: After reading the biography of the pianist Lang Lang, many people may doubt whether children should really be made to undergo such practice. In fact, top athletes are all children from poor families. Without practicing those ten thousand hours, one is certain not to become a master. But the problem is that, considering the factor of opportunity, even practicing those ten thousand hours does not guarantee success.

[Even practicing those ten thousand hours does not guarantee success] Owing to the factor of opportunity, one fails to satisfy the four requirements of deliberate practice and therefore does not succeed. As said above, the four requirements of deliberate practice are: 1. practice only in the “learning zone”; 2. massive repetition; 3. continuously obtain effective feedback; 4. intense mental concentration.
If there is any factor of success that scientists cannot yet explain by postnatal training, it is interest.
Some children seem born interested in a particular field
. Being interested does not necessarily mean one can do it well; even without interest, as long as one is willing to practice, one can train oneself to mastery.
The greatest role of interest is that it makes a person willing to practice in that field.
[The greatest role of interest is that it makes a person willing to practice in that field] Therefore, when you have set your goal and are practicing, you should consciously cultivate your interest,
until you can enjoy the practice
. Interest can be cultivated!
In any case,
deliberate practice is a scientific method

, and it is worth applying to our own professions. Clearly, our professional training does not conform to the characteristics of deliberate practice, and this may be why most people have failed to become world-class masters —
genius comes from deliberate practice!
